basis: New mission, no workbook source. Facts: 2017 '20-30-50' legal target for 2025 (Electricity Act revision); 2024 generation mix 42.4% gas / 39.3% coal / 11.6% renewables / 4.2% nuclear (288 TWh, MOEA/EIA-sourced reporting); solar PV target 20GW by 2025 vs ~14.3GW end-2024 / ~15GW end-2025 (EnergyTrend, pv magazine, ICC Tainan); offshore wind target 5.7GW by 2025 vs ~4.6-4.9GW actual (RECCESSARY, Taiwan News, Norton Rose Fulbright); Taiwan ranked 3rd globally for new offshore wind added in 2025 and 5th for total capacity; MOEA reset the 20% deadline to November 2026 (Eco-Business); wind generation +66% 2023->2024, solar ~45%/wind ~31% of renewable mix; 2050 net-zero pathway targets 60-70% renewables by 2050, 40-55GW installed capacity vs 29GW targeted for 2025 (National Development Council); TSMC ~9% of national electricity (SDxCentral/TrendForce). Register per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md. Drafted with Gemini 3.1 Pro, then substantially rewritten by Claude for CEFR band conformance, factual precision and tone (softened one overstated 'existential threat' claim in the original draft).

slides.1: You can see wind turbines along our western beaches, and solar panels on our classroom roofs. But has Taiwan actually become green, or does it only talk about it?
slides.2: SDG 7 promises affordable, reliable energy for everyone, though today we will not discuss climate change, because that belongs elsewhere. This talk instead is about our targets and our reality.
slides.3: In 2017, Taiwan's lawmakers locked in a 20-30-50 formula for 2025. Renewables would supply 20 percent of the grid, coal 30 percent, and gas the remaining 50 percent.
slides.4: The real numbers from 2024 tell a different story. Renewables have only reached 11.6 percent, which falls far short of the 20 percent goal, while gas and coal still dominate the grid.
slides.5: The solar target was 20 gigawatts by 2025, yet only about 15 have been installed so far. Tighter rules and land disputes have slowed the permitting process across the island.
slides.6: Offshore wind aimed for 5.7 gigawatts, but Taiwan has only reached about 4.9. Rising costs and global supply problems have made recent auctions weaker than planners had hoped.
slides.7: Even though Taiwan missed its own target, the record still looks strong worldwide. Taiwan has ranked third globally for new offshore wind added in 2025, ahead of most nations.
slides.8: The landscape has genuinely changed around us. Solar panels have spread across fish ponds, school roofs and factory buildings, while wind generation has grown by 66 percent in one year.
slides.9: The government has not cancelled its 20 percent goal. Instead, it has pushed the deadline to November 2026, a date that still demands far more power than Taiwan produces right now.
slides.10: Solving the solar delay means reforming the land rules first. Instead of leaving approvals to scattered local offices, the central government could step in so permits move much faster.
slides.11: Winning back investor trust matters just as much for wind power. Instead of holding small, weak auctions, Taiwan should offer bigger contracts that can actually cover today's higher turbine costs.
slides.12: The 2050 plan also counts on hydrogen and geothermal power. Instead of relying only on solar and wind, Taiwan should diversify, though newer options will need more time to mature.
slides.13: Our chip plants use huge amounts of power every single day. If verified green power is not delivered soon, global clients that demand it could simply take their business elsewhere.
slides.14: The pressure is now on that new 2026 date. If this delayed goal slips again, investor trust will weaken further, and weaker trust is exactly what caused the last shortfall.
slides.15: Restoring that trust is not only about money, though money matters too. If wind farms are built too quickly, local communities could feel the disruption first, without gaining much power.
slides.16: These economic and local pressures are all closely connected. If we ignore the communities that host this equipment, public support will fade fast, so the real test is keeping trust.
slides.17: To wrap up, real progress clearly exists across Taiwan today. We have built turbines, spread solar panels, and earned a top-five global ranking, yet our reality sits behind our legal targets.
slides.18: This gap matters to everyone sitting in this room. You are the students who will become the engineers designing the grid connections and storage systems that finally close this divide.
slides.19: Let's study the data much more critically from now on. Stop asking only what was announced, and start asking what has actually been delivered, then join the debates that shape it.
slides.20: Let's carry just one thought forward from today. Governments can always push a deadline back, but our destination should never move, so let's make sure Taiwan actually arrives there.
